title: The Brothers Who Built a Bridge
summary: Two brothers who constantly argue over chores must set aside their rivalry and cooperate to build a simple wooden footbridge so their younger siblings can safely reach school after a flood.
poll: Siblings who argue a lot can never learn to work well together.

versions.title: The Brothers Who Built a Bridge
versions.text:
Saad and Faisal were brothers. They did not get along. They often argued about chores. "Feed the chickens!" Saad would say. "No, you feed them!" Faisal would say back.

Near their house was a small stream. Lama and Zaid walked across it. They went to school this way.

One day, it rained hard. The stream got wide. It got fast too. Lama and Zaid could not cross. They had to walk far around.

Dad said, "Build a bridge, boys."

The brothers argued about the plan. Then they stopped. They worked together instead.

They cut wood. They made planks. They built a strong bridge.

Lama and Zaid crossed the new bridge. They were happy. The brothers felt proud. They learned to work as a team.

versions.title: The Brothers Who Built a Bridge
versions.text:
Saad and Faisal were brothers. They lived on a small farm. They did not get along well. They often argued about chores. "It is your turn to feed the chickens!" Saad would shout. "No, it is your turn!" Faisal would shout back.

Near their house ran a small stream. Every morning, Lama and Zaid crossed it on some flat stones. Then they walked to school.

One week, heavy rain fell for days. The stream grew wide and fast. It covered the flat stones. Lama and Zaid could not cross. They had to walk a long way around.

Their father said, "Boys, I need you to build a bridge over the stream."

At first, the brothers argued about the plan. Saad wanted one idea. Faisal wanted another. Finally, they stopped arguing. They decided to work together.

They cut strong wood. They made planks. Slowly, they built a simple, sturdy footbridge.

Lama and Zaid happily crossed the new bridge. The brothers felt proud. They had learned that working together was much better than arguing.

versions.text:
Saad and Faisal were brothers. They lived on a small farm at the edge of a quiet village. They did not get along especially well, and they argued often about whose turn it was to do chores. "It is your turn to feed the chickens!" Saad would shout. "No, it is your turn to sweep the yard!" Faisal would shout back. The argument would go on for several minutes.

Near their house ran a small, usually gentle stream. Every morning, Lama and Zaid crossed the stream on some flat stones to reach the path to school.

One week, heavy rain fell for several days. The stream grew wide and fast. It completely covered the flat stones the children normally used. Lama and Zaid could no longer cross safely. They had to walk a long way around, arriving tired, muddy, and often late.

Their father noticed how tired the younger children looked. He said, "I need you two to build a simple wooden bridge, so your brother and sister do not have to walk so far."

At first, the brothers argued loudly about how to build it. Saad wanted thick logs laid side by side. Faisal insisted that thin, light planks would work better. Finally, tired of arguing, they decided to actually work together.

They cut strong pieces of wood. They measured carefully. They nailed the pieces into even planks. Slowly, the two brothers built a simple but sturdy footbridge.

The very next morning, Lama and Zaid happily crossed the new bridge. Saad and Faisal felt genuinely proud. They finally understood that working as a team worked far better than constantly arguing.

versions.title: The Brothers Who Built a Bridge
versions.text:
Saad and Faisal were brothers who lived with their family on a modest farm at the edge of a quiet village, surrounded by open fields and scattered trees. The two of them rarely got along, and a persistent rivalry simmered between them, surfacing nearly every day as they argued over whose turn it was to complete the household chores. "It's your turn to feed the chickens!" Saad would shout. "No, it's your turn to sweep the yard!" Faisal would shout back, each one as stubborn as the other, refusing to budge until exhaustion finally forced someone to give in.

Near their house flowed a small stream, ordinarily calm and easy enough to cross. Each morning, their younger siblings, Lama and Zaid, stepped across a line of flat stones spanning the water, continuing along a dirt path toward their school on the far side of the village.

One week, relentless rain fell for several consecutive days. The stream swelled rapidly, submerging the stepping stones the children normally relied upon. Lama and Zaid could no longer cross safely, forcing them to walk a long way around through muddy fields simply to reach school on time, often arriving exhausted and late.

Their father, noticing how worn out the younger children looked each afternoon, finally said, "Saad, Faisal, I need the two of you to collaborate and construct a simple wooden bridge over the stream, so your brother and sister no longer have to walk so far every day."

At first, the brothers merely argued about how to build it, each convinced his own idea was the only sensible approach. Saad insisted on thick logs laid side by side, while Faisal argued that thin, light planks would prove easier to carry and equally strong once properly secured. Neither wanted to yield, until they recognized that their rivalry was simply wasting time while their siblings continued to struggle.

Eventually, they agreed to a practical compromise, combining elements of both approaches into a single, improved plan. They measured the stream's width, cut sturdy lengths of wood accordingly, and carefully nailed each plank into place, inspecting their progress as they worked.

The following morning, Lama and Zaid crossed the new, sturdy bridge happily, scarcely dampening their shoes despite the stream's continued current. Saad and Faisal felt genuinely proud of what their collaboration had achieved, recognizing at last that cooperating produced results neither rivalry nor stubbornness ever could.

keyWords.definition: a structure built over a river, stream, or road so people or things can cross it
keyWords.example: We walked over the old stone bridge to reach the park.
Children often play near the stream behind the school.

keyWords.definition: to talk angrily with someone because you disagree about something
keyWords.example: The two friends began to argue about which movie to watch.

keyWords.definition: a small job that needs to be done regularly, often at home
keyWords.example: Washing the dishes is one of my daily chores.

keyWords.definition: a boy or man who has the same parents as you
keyWords.example: My brother and I share a room.

questions.stem: What is this story mostly about?
options: Two brothers who argue, then build a bridge together
A young girl who walks to school alone each day
A family that decides to move to a new village
Two brothers who work hard to build a chicken coop
questions.why: The story is about Saad and Faisal, who argue often but finally work together to build a bridge for their younger siblings.

wrong.B: The story is about two brothers, not a girl walking alone.
wrong.C: The family does not move to a new village.
wrong.D: The brothers build a bridge, not a chicken coop.

questions.stem: Why could Lama and Zaid not cross the stream after the heavy rain?
options: The small stream had completely frozen solid
A large tree had fallen right across the path
The flat stones were covered by fast water
Their school shoes were much too big
questions.why: In the story, the stream got wide and fast, so the children could not cross.

wrong.A: The story does not say the stream froze.
wrong.B: No fallen tree is mentioned in the story.
wrong.D: The problem was the flooded stream, not their shoes.

questions.stem: What did the brothers' father ask them to do?
options: Feed the farm chickens every single day
Walk Lama and Zaid all the way to school
Go and buy some new flat stones
Build a wooden bridge over the stream
questions.why: The father asked Saad and Faisal to build a simple wooden bridge over the stream.

wrong.A: Feeding chickens was just one of their usual chores, not what the father asked for here.
wrong.B: The father did not ask them to walk the younger children to school.
wrong.C: The father did not ask them to buy new stones.

questions.stem: In the story, to argue means to —
options: to talk or shout angrily because you disagree
to quickly agree with what someone says
to walk somewhere together with a friend
to build something carefully out of wood
questions.why: The brothers argue, or shout angrily, because they disagree about chores and about how to build the bridge.

wrong.B: Arguing is not the same as quickly agreeing.
wrong.C: Arguing is not about walking together.
wrong.D: Arguing is not the same as building something.

questions.stem: Why did Saad and Faisal argue about chores?
options: Neither wanted to do more work than the other
They both really wanted to go to school
They did not like having any chickens
They both wanted to cross the small stream
questions.why: Each brother wanted the other to feed the chickens or sweep the yard, showing neither wanted to do more work than the other.

wrong.B: Going to school is not mentioned as the reason for their chore arguments.
wrong.C: The story does not say they disliked chickens.
wrong.D: Crossing the stream is not related to their chore arguments.

questions.stem: Why did the brothers finally stop arguing about the bridge?
options: Their father simply built it instead of the boys
Arguing was wasting time while the flood continued
It finally stopped raining that same day at noon
Lama and Zaid quickly learned how to swim in the river
questions.why: The brothers realized their arguing was only wasting time while their siblings still could not get to school safely.

wrong.A: The father asked them to build it, but they built it themselves.
wrong.C: The story does not say the rain simply stopped and solved the problem.
wrong.D: The story does not say Lama and Zaid learned to swim.

questions.stem: What happened after the brothers worked together instead of arguing?

The farm's chickens suddenly ran far away
The flooded stream completely dried up
The new bridge quickly fell back down

wrong.B: The story does not mention the chickens running away.
wrong.C: The stream was still flowing, not dried up.
wrong.D: The bridge held up and did not fall down.

questions.stem: Why does the author show the brothers arguing at the start of the story?

To show that they never liked doing chores
To carefully explain how to feed chickens
To mainly describe what the village looks like
questions.why: Showing the brothers arguing at the start helps readers see how much they changed by working together at the end.

wrong.B: The story is not really about whether they liked chores.
wrong.C: The story does not explain how to feed chickens.
wrong.D: The arguing at the start is not mainly about describing the village.

LOW.prompt: Do you think Saad and Faisal were right to stop arguing and work together? Explain your answer using at least two facts from the story.
checklist: I clearly said what I think.
I used at least two facts from the story.
I wrote complete sentences with capital letters and periods.
LOW.modelAnswer: I think Saad and Faisal were right to stop arguing and work together. At first they argued about chores and about how to build the bridge, which wasted time while Lama and Zaid still could not get to school. Once the brothers worked together, they built a strong bridge, and Lama and Zaid could cross safely the very next morning. Working together helped them solve the problem much faster than arguing ever could.

keyWords.definition: to work together with someone to get something done
keyWords.example: The two classmates had to cooperate to finish the science project on time.

keyWords.definition: a long, flat piece of wood used for building
keyWords.example: The workers laid a long plank across the ditch so people could walk over it.

keyWords.definition: a narrow way for walking from one place to another
keyWords.example: A sandy path led from the house down to the beach.

keyWords.definition: unwilling to change your mind or give in, even when it might be a good idea
keyWords.example: The stubborn goat refused to move, no matter how hard we pulled.

keyWords.definition: the combined effort of people working together toward a shared goal
keyWords.example: Good teamwork helped the class finish cleaning the garden quickly.

questions.stem: Which sentence best states the central idea of the story?
options: Two stubborn brothers cooperate to build a needed bridge
A simple story about raising chickens on a farm in spring
A path that quietly disappears forever one night in the dark
Two brothers who never speak to each other again after the flood
questions.why: The story is about Saad and Faisal setting aside their stubbornness to cooperate and build a bridge so Lama and Zaid can safely reach school.

wrong.B: Chickens are mentioned only as one of the brothers' chores.
wrong.C: The path itself does not disappear in the story.
wrong.D: By the end, the brothers work and feel proud together.

questions.stem: Why couldn't Lama and Zaid use the path to school after the heavy rain?

wrong.C: The story does not say school was closed.
wrong.D: The father did not forbid them from going; the flood stopped them.

questions.stem: What two different plans did Saad and Faisal first propose for the bridge?

wrong.B: Digging a tunnel or filling in the stream is not mentioned.

questions.stem: In the story, stubborn means —

feeling quite tired after hard farm work
being very skilled at building things well
refusing to change your mind or give in
questions.why: The brothers are described as stubborn because each refused to give in to the other's plan at first.

wrong.A: Stubborn is the opposite of easily changing your mind.
wrong.B: Stubborn does not describe feeling tired.
wrong.C: Stubborn is about attitude, not building skill.

questions.stem: Why did the brothers eventually stop arguing about which plan to use?
options: Their father simply chose a plan for them in the end
They saw their arguing was wasting precious time
The two brothers simply ran out of wood to build it
Lama and Zaid quietly built it themselves at night
questions.why: The brothers realized that their arguing was simply wasting time while their younger siblings continued to struggle each morning.

wrong.A: The father asked them to build it but did not choose the plan himself.
wrong.C: There is no mention of running out of wood.
wrong.D: Lama and Zaid did not build the bridge themselves.

questions.stem: What can you infer about Saad and Faisal's relationship by the end of the story?

They now argue even more than before this happened
They decide never to do any chores together again
They decide to move far away from the farm

wrong.B: The story shows the opposite: less arguing, not more.
wrong.C: There is no mention of avoiding chores together in the future.
wrong.D: The brothers stay on the farm; they do not move away.

questions.stem: Why was the new bridge able to keep Lama and Zaid's shoes from getting wet?

It had completely stopped raining by then
The bridge was sturdy and built above the water
The flooded stream had simply disappeared

wrong.A: The story says Lama and Zaid crossed the bridge themselves, not that they were carried.
wrong.B: The stream was still flowing fast even after the bridge was built.
wrong.D: The stream did not disappear; it kept flowing under the bridge.

questions.stem: How does the author organize events in this story?
options: By comparing two completely different villages near the river
In time order: arguing, the flood, the request, the work
By simply listing different types of wood used for the bridge
By describing the farm from present back to past events
questions.why: The story follows events in time order, from the brothers' usual arguing, to the flood, to the father's request, to building the bridge, and finally the happy result.

wrong.A: The story does not compare two villages.
wrong.C: The story is a narrative, not a list of wood types.
wrong.D: The story moves forward in time, not backward.

MID.prompt: Explain how Saad and Faisal's relationship changed from the beginning of the story to the end. Use at least two details from the story.
checklist: I explained how the brothers' relationship changed.
I used at least two details from the story.
I organized my ideas in a clear order.
MID.modelAnswer: At the beginning of the story, Saad and Faisal argued constantly, even about small chores like feeding the chickens or sweeping the yard. When their father asked them to build a bridge, they still argued at first, each insisting on his own plan for using logs or planks. By the end of the story, though, they had learned to cooperate, combining their ideas and working together to build a sturdy bridge for Lama and Zaid. Their relationship changed from constant arguing to real teamwork, and they both felt proud of what they built together.

keyWords.definition: to work jointly with one or more people on a shared task or project
keyWords.example: Scientists from different countries often collaborate on important research.

keyWords.definition: strongly and solidly built, not likely to break or fall apart
keyWords.example: The old wooden table was sturdy enough to hold heavy boxes.

keyWords.definition: an agreement reached when each side gives up part of what it wanted
keyWords.example: After some discussion, the two neighbors reached a compromise about the fence.

keyWords.definition: to build something by putting its parts together
keyWords.example: Workers used steel beams to construct the new building.

keyWords.definition: a state of competing with someone, often over a long time
keyWords.example: A friendly rivalry between the two soccer teams made every match exciting.

questions.stem: Which statement best captures the central idea of the story?
options: A rivalry ends once two brothers learn to collaborate
The story is mainly about different kinds of wood
Saad and Faisal never resolve their disagreement
The story mostly focuses on one village's history
questions.why: The story centers on Saad and Faisal setting aside their rivalry to collaborate on constructing a sturdy bridge that solves their siblings' problem.

wrong.B: Wood is mentioned only as a building material, not the main topic.
wrong.C: The brothers do resolve their disagreement by reaching a compromise.
wrong.D: The story is a narrative about one family event, not village history.

questions.stem: Why did Lama and Zaid have to take a much longer route to school?
options: Their school had suddenly moved to a new building
The flooded stream had submerged the stepping stones
Their father had forbidden them from using the stream
The dirt path had been formally closed by the village

wrong.A: The story does not mention the school moving.
wrong.C: The father did not forbid the stream; the flood made it unsafe.
wrong.D: The story does not mention the path being officially closed.

questions.stem: What compromise did the brothers eventually reach about building the bridge?
options: They abandoned the whole bridge project entirely
They decided to use only Saad's original plan
They asked their father to simply decide for them
They combined parts of both of their ideas

wrong.A: The brothers completed the bridge rather than abandoning it.
wrong.B: They did not use only Saad's plan; they blended both ideas.
wrong.C: The father asked them to build the bridge but did not design it for them.

questions.stem: In the story, to collaborate means to —
options: to argue persistently about a single decision
to work together toward a shared goal
to firmly refuse any outside help offered
to compete against someone for a prize
questions.why: The brothers collaborate, meaning they work together, once they set aside their rivalry to build the bridge.

wrong.A: Collaborating is the opposite of arguing persistently.
wrong.C: Collaborating involves accepting help, not refusing it.
wrong.D: Collaborating is working together, not competing.

questions.stem: What does the brothers' initial insistence on two different plans suggest about their rivalry?
options: It had almost no real effect on their work
It made the problem harder to solve efficiently
It actually helped them build the bridge faster
It made their father quite proud at first
questions.why: Their rivalry over competing plans delayed progress, since neither brother would yield until they recognized the time being wasted.

wrong.A: Their rivalry clearly slowed down the process at first.
wrong.C: The rivalry slowed them down rather than speeding up the work.
wrong.D: The father's request came because the children were struggling, not because he was already proud of an ongoing rivalry.

questions.stem: Put these events in the correct order.
options: Stream floods, father asks for a bridge, compromise, done
Father asks for a bridge, stream floods, compromise, done
Brothers compromise, stream floods, done, father asks
Bridge is done, compromise, stream floods, father asks
questions.why: First the stream floods, then the father asks the brothers to build a bridge, then they reach a compromise, and finally the bridge is finished.

wrong.B: The father only asks them to build a bridge after the stream floods.
wrong.C: The brothers cannot compromise about the bridge before the stream has even flooded.
wrong.D: The bridge cannot be finished before the flood and the father's request occur.

questions.stem: What does the brothers' experience suggest about resolving disagreements?
options: Ongoing rivalry always produces the very best results
Collaborating can work better than acting alone
Reaching any compromise is never worth the effort
Only ever one single person's plan should be used
questions.why: By setting aside their rivalry and collaborating on a compromise, the brothers built a bridge better than either of their original separate plans.

wrong.A: Their rivalry actually slowed down progress rather than producing the best results.
wrong.C: The compromise is exactly what allowed them to succeed.
wrong.D: The brothers combined both of their plans rather than using only one.

questions.stem: Why does the author end the story by saying the lesson extended beyond the bridge itself?
options: To suggest that the brothers forgot the lesson quickly
To show collaboration could help with future challenges
To argue that building bridges is quite unimportant
To show that chores no longer mattered to them
questions.why: By noting that the lesson extended beyond the bridge, the author emphasizes that the brothers' new understanding of collaboration would help them with future challenges, including everyday chores.

wrong.A: The ending shows the lesson stayed with them, not that they forgot it.
wrong.C: The bridge itself was clearly important, since it solved a real problem.
wrong.D: The story suggests chores became easier to divide fairly, not unimportant.

HIGH.prompt: The story suggests that collaboration can solve problems that rivalry cannot. Do you agree or disagree? Support your argument with evidence from the story.
checklist: I supported my position with specific evidence from the story.
I addressed at least one point someone might make against my view.
HIGH.modelAnswer: I agree that collaboration can solve problems that rivalry cannot. In the story, Saad and Faisal's rivalry over whose plan was better only wasted time while Lama and Zaid kept struggling to reach school safely. It was only once the brothers set their rivalry aside and reached a compromise, combining both of their ideas, that they actually finished a sturdy bridge. Someone might argue that competition can sometimes push people to work harder, but in this case the brothers' competing plans only delayed the solution; it was their decision to collaborate that solved the real problem their family faced.
